items.prompt: What does lower_bound(target) return in ascending data?

options.text: The first index whose value is strictly greater than target.
The first index whose value is greater than or equal to target, or n if no such index exists.
The last index whose value is less than or equal to target.
Any index equal to target.

feedback.reason: Lower bound locates the insertion boundary before all values that are not less than target.

blocks.text: Lower bound is a false-to-true partition

In ascending data, the predicate value >= target is false for an initial prefix and true for the remaining suffix. lower_bound(target) returns the boundary between those regions: the first true index.

items: If target occurs, this is its first equal position because equality satisfies >=.
If target is absent inside the value range, this is the index of the first larger value and therefore the sorted insertion position.
If every value is smaller, the true suffix is empty and the boundary is the sentinel n.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: For [1, 4, 4, 9], lower_bound(4) = 1, lower_bound(6) = 3, and lower_bound(10) = 4 = n.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.first_gt: Strictly greater uses the predicate value > target and defines upper_bound, which skips every value equal to target.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.last_le: This asks for a predecessor at the right edge of the <= region; it is derived as upper_bound(target) - 1 when that region is non-empty.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.any_equal: An arbitrary equal index does not guarantee the leftmost boundary, and no equal index exists when target is absent even though lower_bound remains defined.

items.prompt: What does upper_bound(target) return in ascending data?

options.text: The first index whose value is greater than or equal to target.
The last index equal to target.
The first index whose value is strictly greater than target, or n if no such index exists.
Any index whose value is greater than target.

feedback.reason: Upper bound separates values less than or equal to target from strictly greater values.

blocks.text: Upper bound moves equality to the left partition

upper_bound(target) searches the monotonic predicate value > target. Every value <= target belongs to the false prefix, including all copies equal to target; strictly greater values form the true suffix.

items: The answer is the first true index, so it is immediately after the final value <= target.
If no value is strictly greater, the true suffix is empty and the returned boundary is n.
Unlike a last-equal query, upper_bound remains meaningful when target is absent.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: For [1, 4, 4, 9], upper_bound(4) = 3, upper_bound(6) = 3, and upper_bound(9) = 4 = n.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.first_ge: Greater than or equal makes equality true and therefore stops at the first equal value; that is lower_bound, not upper_bound.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.last_equal: Upper bound is a boundary one position after the final equal value, and it is still defined when target has no equal value.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.any_greater: A later greater index satisfies the predicate but does not identify its first true position, so it is not the required partition boundary.

items.prompt: The sorted array is [1, 2, 2, 2, 5]. What are lower_bound(2) and upper_bound(2)?

options.text: 1 and 3.
2 and 4.
0 and 5.
1 and 4.

feedback.reason: The equal-value range is the half-open interval [lower_bound, upper_bound).

blocks.text: Apply both strictness rules
Index the array as 0:1, 1:2, 2:2, 3:2, 4:5. lower_bound(2) asks for the first value >= 2, so the first true index is 1.

items: Values at indices 0 through 0 are < 2; values from index 1 onward are >= 2. Therefore lower_bound(2) = 1.
Values at indices 0 through 3 are <= 2; index 4 is the first value > 2. Therefore upper_bound(2) = 4.
The half-open interval [1, 4) contains indices 1, 2, and 3—exactly all three copies of 2.

blocks.title: Avoid the last-index confusion
blocks.text: Index 3 is the last equal element, but upper_bound is the exclusive boundary after it, index 4.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_three: Index 3 is the last equal value, not the first greater value.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two_four: Lower bound must return the first equal position.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero_five: Those are the full-array boundaries, not the target boundaries.

items.prompt: How can the number of occurrences of target in sorted data be computed from boundaries?

options.text: lower_bound(target) - upper_bound(target).
upper_bound(target) - lower_bound(target).
upper_bound(target) + lower_bound(target).
Return 1 whenever any exact match exists.

feedback.reason: The half-open equal range contains exactly upper - lower indices.

blocks.text: Turn the equal block into a range length
All copies of target are contiguous in sorted data. lower_bound(target) is the first index in that block, and upper_bound(target) is the first index after it, so the equal block is [lower, upper).

items: A half-open integer interval [a, b) contains b - a indices.
For [1, 2, 2, 2, 5], the equal block is [1, 4), so the count is 4 - 1 = 3.
If target is absent, the >= and > predicates switch at the same insertion point; lower = upper and the subtraction returns 0.

blocks.title: Transfer rule
blocks.text: Whenever two boundaries delimit a contiguous half-open result range, its cardinality is right boundary minus left boundary.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.lower_minus_upper: Because lower <= upper, reversing the endpoints produces zero or a negative number rather than the nonnegative range length.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.upper_plus_lower: Adding absolute index positions does not count how many indices lie between them; range length comes from their difference.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.any_match: An exact-match flag distinguishes zero from at least one but cannot determine how many duplicate copies occupy the equal block.

items.prompt: What should lower_bound(target) return when every array value is smaller than target?

options.text: n - 1, the final valid index.
n, the insertion position after the final element.

feedback.reason: The insertion boundary may be one past the final valid index.

blocks.text: The true suffix is empty
lower_bound uses the predicate value >= target. If every array value is smaller than target, that predicate is false at every valid index, so there is no in-array first true index.

items: The canonical boundary domain is [0, n], not only the element-index range [0, n - 1].
The sentinel n represents the transition immediately after the false prefix containing the entire array.
Inserting target at n appends it after every smaller value and preserves ascending order.

blocks.title: Do not dereference the sentinel
blocks.text: n is a valid returned boundary but not a valid array index. Callers must check lower < n before reading nums[lower].

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.n_minus_one: The final valid index still contains a value < target, so it does not satisfy the >= predicate and is not the insertion boundary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.minus_one: The canonical lower-bound contract returns a position in [0, n]; it represents no in-array true value with n, not -1.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero: Position 0 is before every smaller value, so inserting target there would break ascending order unless the array is empty, where 0 also equals n.

items.prompt: What should lower_bound(target) return when every array value is greater than target?

options.text: n.

feedback.reason: The first position already satisfies the lower-bound predicate.

blocks.text: The true suffix begins immediately
If every array value is greater than target, then every value also satisfies value >= target. The lower-bound predicate is true starting at the first valid index.

items: There is no false prefix of smaller values.
The first true index is therefore 0.
Inserting target at 0 places it before every greater value and preserves ascending order.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: For [5, 8, 11] and target 3, each value is >= 3, so lower_bound(3) = 0.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one: Index 0 already satisfies value >= target, so index 1 cannot be the first true position.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.n_minus_one: The last index may satisfy the predicate, but lower_bound requires the first satisfying index, which is 0 here.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.n: The sentinel n is used only when no array index satisfies the predicate; here every index does, beginning at 0.

options.text: Equality is never a valid lower-bound condition.
An earlier equal value may still exist in the left region.
Lower bound always lies to the right of an equal value.
Duplicates make the array unsorted.

feedback.reason: A matching midpoint is a valid candidate but may not be the first valid candidate.

blocks.text: Equality proves validity, not minimality
lower_bound searches for the first index satisfying nums[i] >= target. When nums[mid] == target, mid satisfies that predicate, but duplicates may make an earlier index satisfy it too.

items: In [1, 2, 2, 2, 5], an initial midpoint can be index 2, where equality holds.
Returning 2 would be wrong because index 1 is the first value >= 2.
The true branch sets right = mid, preserving mid as a possible returned boundary while continuing to test whether the transition occurs earlier.

blocks.title: Exact search asks a different question
blocks.text: Returning on equality is valid when any matching index satisfies the result contract. It is invalid when the contract asks for the leftmost boundary.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.equal_never_valid: Equality does satisfy nums[mid] >= target, so mid is valid; the missing fact is whether it is the first valid index.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.must_search_right: A matching midpoint is already valid, and the only unresolved possibility is an earlier valid index on the left.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.duplicates_unsorted: Ascending order allows equal adjacent values; duplicates preserve monotonicity but make an arbitrary equality hit insufficient.

items.prompt: Provided at least one sorted-array value is <= target, how can its last such index be derived from upper_bound?

options.text: lower_bound(target) + 1.
upper_bound(target).
upper_bound(target) - 1.
Always return n.

feedback.reason: Upper bound is the first position outside the <= target region.

blocks.text: Take the predecessor of the first greater value
upper_bound(target) is the first index whose value is > target. Therefore every index before it has value <= target, and the index immediately before it is the last member of that region.

items: For [2, 4, 4, 7] and target 4, upper_bound(4) = 3 because index 3 is the first value > 4.
Subtracting one gives index 2, the final value <= 4.
If upper_bound(target) = 0, no predecessor exists; the prompt excludes that case by guaranteeing at least one value <= target.

blocks.title: Predecessor rule
blocks.text: The last index satisfying a prefix predicate is one less than the first index outside that prefix, provided the prefix is non-empty.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.lower_plus_one: lower_bound marks the first value >= target, so adding one neither identifies the end of duplicates nor the last value below target in general.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.upper_itself: upper_bound is the first strictly greater position and is therefore already outside the <= target region.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.n_always: n - 1 is the result only when every array value is <= target; otherwise the first greater boundary occurs earlier.

items.prompt: Provided at least one sorted-array value is < target, how can its last such index be derived from lower_bound?

options.text: upper_bound(target) - 1.
lower_bound(target).
Always return 0.
lower_bound(target) - 1, when lower_bound is greater than zero.

feedback.reason: Lower bound is the first position outside the < target region.

blocks.text: Take the predecessor of the first greater-or-equal value
lower_bound(target) is the first index whose value is >= target. Every index before it is therefore strictly smaller than target, so the predecessor is the last strictly smaller index.

items: For [2, 4, 4, 7] and target 4, lower_bound(4) = 1.
Index 0 is the predecessor and contains 2 < 4, so the answer is 1 - 1 = 0.
If lower_bound(target) = 0, no smaller value exists and subtracting one would produce an invalid index.

blocks.title: Strictness selects the boundary
blocks.text: Use lower_bound - 1 for the last value < target. Use upper_bound - 1 for the last value <= target.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.upper_minus_one: upper_bound skips values equal to target, so its predecessor is the last <= target rather than the last strictly smaller value.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.lower_itself: lower_bound is the first position outside the < target prefix, so it cannot itself be the final member of that prefix.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero_always: Index 0 is correct only when exactly the first element is below target; the smaller-value prefix may be empty or contain many indices.

items.prompt: The target is absent from sorted data. How are lower_bound(target) and upper_bound(target) related?

options.text: Lower bound is always strictly smaller.
They are equal at the target's insertion position.
Upper bound is smaller than lower bound.
Both must be -1.

feedback.reason: With no values equal to target, the >= and > predicates change at the same position.

blocks.text: Without equality, strictness makes no partition difference
lower_bound uses value >= target and upper_bound uses value > target. These predicates differ only at values exactly equal to target.

items: When target is absent, every value is either < target or > target; no index exposes the predicates' equality difference.
Both first-true searches therefore transition at the first greater value, which is the sorted insertion position.
For [1, 4, 7] and target 5, both boundaries are 2. For target 9, both are n = 3.

blocks.title: Count consequence
blocks.text: The equal-value range [lower, upper) is empty, so upper - lower = 0 without requiring a special not-found sentinel.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.lower_less: lower_bound is strictly smaller only when one or more equal values lie between the two boundaries; absence removes that gap.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.upper_less: The predicate > target implies >= target, so its first true point cannot occur before lower_bound.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.both_minus_one: Canonical bounds return an insertion position in [0, n], including 0 and n; they do not use -1 for absence.

items.prompt: For an array of length n >= 2, which are legal lower-bound return values? Select all that apply.

options.text: -1 under the canonical [0, n) contract.
n.
Any index from 1 through n - 1.

feedback.reason: Lower bound returns an insertion boundary in the closed numeric range [0, n].

blocks.text: There are n + 1 insertion boundaries
An n-element array has a legal insertion position before index 0, between each adjacent pair, and after index n - 1. Numbered as boundaries, these are exactly 0 through n.

items: 0 occurs when the first element already satisfies value >= target.
Any position 1 through n - 1 occurs when the transition lies inside the array.
n occurs when every element is < target and is a valid boundary even though it is not an element index.
-1 lies outside the canonical boundary domain and is unnecessary for representing absence.

blocks.title: Boundary versus element
blocks.text: Always validate 0 <= result <= n before treating a bound as a position. Validate result < n separately before dereferencing the array.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.minus_one: The canonical contract represents every outcome with a boundary from 0 through n; -1 is outside that domain and cannot be an insertion position.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.zero: The first array index may already satisfy value >= target, making the beginning boundary the first true position.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.middle: For n >= 2, the false-to-true transition can occur between existing elements at any internal index.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.n: If no element satisfies value >= target, the transition is the exclusive sentinel immediately after the array.

items.prompt: Which queries can be answered using lower or upper boundaries? Select all that apply.

options.text: Find where target can be inserted while preserving order.
Count occurrences of target.
Find any target in arbitrary unsorted data without preprocessing.
Find the last value less than or equal to target.

feedback.reason: Boundary searches expose ordered partition points that support several derived queries.

blocks.text: Map each query to a monotonic partition
Ascending order makes predicates such as value >= target and value > target change from false to true at most once. A boundary search can find that transition and derived queries can use it.

items: Insertion position: lower_bound is the first index where target can appear before equal values.
Occurrence count: upper_bound - lower_bound is the length of the equal block.
Last value <= target: upper_bound - 1 is the predecessor of the first greater value when one exists.
Arbitrary unsorted data has no contiguous false/true partition by index, so these searches are not directly legal without preprocessing.

blocks.title: Legality test
blocks.text: Before applying a bound, state the index predicate and verify that its truth values form one false prefix followed by one true suffix.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.arbitrary_unsorted: Without sorted or otherwise monotonic structure, a midpoint result cannot eliminate an entire side, so lower or upper bound may skip the target.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.insertion: lower_bound returns the first value >= target, so inserting there preserves order and places the new value before existing equals.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.count_equal: All equal values occupy [lower_bound, upper_bound), whose length is upper minus lower.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.last_le: upper_bound is the first value > target, so its predecessor is the final value <= target when that predecessor exists.

items.prompt: Which tests are important for lower and upper bound implementations? Select all that apply.

options.text: Target absent between two existing values.
Only one unique target located initially at mid.
Target smaller than all values and larger than all values.
All array values equal target.

feedback.reason: Boundary tests must exercise duplicate ranges, absence, and both sentinels.

blocks.text: Test where the two predicates differ and where they coincide

A correct implementation must preserve both strictness rules and every legal boundary in [0, n]. Tests should force the transition to the beginning, middle, and end and should include repeated equality.

items: Absent between values: lower and upper must coincide at an internal insertion point.
All values equal target: lower must be 0 and upper must be n, exposing equality handling at both extremes.
Target below all values and above all values: exercises boundary results 0 and n.
Also useful in implementation tests: empty, singleton, duplicate runs at one edge, and transitions beside a two-element interval.

blocks.title: Why one midpoint hit is weak evidence
blocks.text: Returning immediately on equality can pass a unique middle-target case while still failing every duplicate-edge requirement.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_unique_mid: An immediate unique match exercises neither duplicate strictness nor the 0 and n sentinel boundaries, so it cannot validate a bound implementation alone.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.target_absent_between: With no equal value, >= and > change at the same internal insertion point, so both bounds must return it.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.all_equal: Equality must make lower_bound stop at 0 while upper_bound moves past the entire run to n.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.outside_both: These cases force the first-true boundary to the two extreme legal results, 0 and n.

items.prompt: Which predicate-to-boundary mappings are correct? Select all that apply.

First value > target corresponds to upper_bound.

feedback.reason: Boundary definitions can be composed through predecessor relationships.

blocks.text: Match strictness on both sides of the boundary

lower_bound is the first index outside the < target prefix; upper_bound is the first index outside the <= target prefix. Taking a predecessor moves from an exclusive boundary back to the final element inside its prefix.

items: First >= target is lower_bound by definition.
First > target is upper_bound by definition.
Last < target is lower_bound - 1 when lower_bound > 0.
Last <= target is upper_bound - 1 when upper_bound > 0; using lower_bound would stop before equal values.

blocks.title: Duplicate counterexample
blocks.text: For [1, 2, 2, 5] and target 2, lower_bound - 1 = 0 points to the last value < 2, while upper_bound - 1 = 2 points to the last value <= 2.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.last_le_lower: lower_bound - 1 is the last value strictly below target; when equals exist, it lies before them and therefore is not the last value <= target.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.first_ge: The predicate value >= target changes from false to true exactly at lower_bound.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.first_gt: The predicate value > target changes from false to true exactly at upper_bound.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.last_lt: lower_bound is the first position not in the < target prefix, so its predecessor is that prefix's final index when it exists.

items.prompt: Inside a lower-bound loop after the guard left < right succeeds, arrange one iteration over [left, right).

elements.text: Compute a midpoint in the non-empty half-open interval.
If true set right = mid; otherwise set left = mid + 1.

feedback.reason: The predicate is false before the lower bound and true from the lower bound onward.

blocks.text: Search the first value greater than or equal to target

After left < right succeeds, lower-biased mid lies inside [left, right). The invariant says every index before left is < target and every index at or after right is >= target; n is allowed as a vacuous true-side sentinel.
Iteration and trace

items: Compute mid = left + floor((right - left) / 2), so left <= mid < right.
Evaluate nums[mid] >= target.
If true, set right = mid: mid remains the possible returned boundary. If false, set left = mid + 1 because every earlier index is also too small.
Repeat until left == right; the preserved partition then makes that boundary lower_bound.

blocks.title: Trace [1, 2, 2, 5] for target 2
blocks.text: Start [0, 4): mid 2 is true, so right = 2. Then mid 1 is true, so right = 1. Mid 0 is false, so left = 1. Convergence returns the first equal index 1.

items.prompt: Inside an upper-bound loop after the guard left < right succeeds, arrange one iteration over [left, right).

elements.text: If true set right = mid; otherwise set left = mid + 1.

feedback.reason: Upper bound searches the first true position of value > target.

blocks.text: Search the first value strictly greater than target
After left < right succeeds, upper_bound uses the predicate nums[mid] > target. Its false prefix contains every value <= target, so equality follows the same branch as a smaller value.
Iteration and trace

items: Compute a lower-biased midpoint inside [left, right).
Evaluate nums[mid] > target.
If true, set right = mid because this may be the first greater index. Otherwise set left = mid + 1, discarding a value that is <= target.
At left == right, return the converged boundary; n is valid when no value is greater.

blocks.title: Trace [1, 2, 2, 5] for target 2
blocks.text: Start [0, 4): mid 2 equals target, so left = 3. Mid 3 contains 5 > 2, so right = 3. Convergence returns 3, immediately after both copies.

items.prompt: Arrange an occurrence-count algorithm that avoids a second boundary search when target is absent.

elements.text: If lower == n or nums[lower] != target, return 0.
Return upper - lower as the count.

feedback.reason: Lower bound first proves absence cheaply; only a present target needs upper bound to delimit the equal range.

blocks.text: Use lower bound as both boundary and presence check
lower_bound(target) returns the first index that could contain target. If that boundary is n or its value is not equal to target, sorted order proves target is absent and the count is zero.
Dependency order

items: Compute lower = lower_bound(target).
Check lower before dereferencing: if lower == n or nums[lower] != target, return 0.
Otherwise compute upper = upper_bound(target), the first index after the equal block.
Return upper - lower, the length of the half-open equal range [lower, upper).

blocks.title: The optimization does not change the bound
blocks.text: Absent targets use one O(log n) search; present targets use two. Both paths are O(log n), and the early check prevents an unnecessary second search.

items.prompt: Which postconditions together prove that p is lower_bound(target) in ascending data? Select all that apply.

options.text: Check 0 <= p <= n.
Verify every index before p has value < target.
Require p < n and nums[p] == target.
Verify p == n or nums[p] >= target.

feedback.reason: A boundary result is proven by the partition on both sides.

blocks.text: Three postconditions characterize lower bound

lower_bound is a boundary rather than necessarily a matching element. Its proof must establish a legal boundary, exclude every earlier position, and show that the boundary itself is valid unless it is the end sentinel.

items: 0 <= p <= n proves p is an allowed insertion boundary.
Every index before p has value < target, so no earlier boundary can satisfy value >= target.
p == n or nums[p] >= target proves p is the first satisfying index when one exists, with n covering the all-smaller case.
Requiring nums[p] == target would reject valid insertion boundaries for absent targets.

blocks.title: Absent-target example
blocks.text: For [1, 4, 7], target 5, and p = 2: p is in [0, 3], indices 0 and 1 contain values < 5, and nums[2] = 7 >= 5. Therefore p = 2 is lower_bound even without equality.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.exact_match: lower_bound is also the insertion position for an absent target and may equal n, so exact equality is not a required postcondition.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.range: The canonical boundary domain is [0, n]; a value outside it cannot be a valid lower-bound result.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.left_partition: If every earlier value is < target, no earlier index can satisfy the lower-bound predicate.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.right_condition: The boundary must satisfy value >= target when it is an array index, while n represents the case where no such index exists.

items.prompt: Two iterative boundary searches compute lower_bound and upper_bound on n sorted values. Select total time and auxiliary-space complexity.
constraints: Each search performs O(1) work per iteration.

feedback.reason: Two logarithmic searches still sum to O(log n).

blocks.text: Add the two search costs

Each boundary search halves a domain of n indices. After k iterations the remaining size is at most about n / 2^k, so each search performs O(log n) iterations and O(log n) total work under the O(1)-per-iteration premise.
Combine time and storage

items: Time: O(log n) + O(log n) = O(2 log n) = O(log n).
Space: the searches run sequentially and reuse a constant number of boundary, midpoint, and result variables.
No recursive frames or input-sized auxiliary structure are included, so peak auxiliary space is O(1), not the sum of space over time.

blocks.title: Constant repetitions do not multiply the order
blocks.text: A fixed number of logarithmic searches remains logarithmic. If the number of searches were an input q, the query term would instead be O(q log n).

items.prompt: An unsorted array of n values is sorted once, then q lower-bound queries are answered. Select total time and additional space assuming an in-place O(n log n) sort.
constraints: Each query uses iterative binary search.
The input may be reordered by the contract.
The specified in-place sort uses O(1) auxiliary space; output storage is not counted.

time: O(n log n + q log n)
O(n log n + q log n)

time.sort_plus_queries: O(n log n + q log n)

feedback.reason: The preprocessing cost and all query costs must both be included.

blocks.text: Separate one-time preprocessing from repeated queries
Binary-search boundaries require sorted data. The prompt permits reordering, so the array is sorted once for O(n log n), after which each of q independent lower-bound queries costs O(log n).
Add the lifecycle costs

items: Preprocessing: O(n log n).
Queries: q times O(log n), giving O(q log n).
Total: O(n log n + q log n). Omitting the sorting term would describe only the post-preprocessing phase.
The stated sort uses O(1) auxiliary space and iterative search uses O(1); sequential phases therefore have O(1) peak additional space.

blocks.title: Scope of the space claim
blocks.text: The O(1) result follows from the prompt's explicit sort-space guarantee, not from the word “in-place” alone. A recursive in-place sort could still retain O(log n) call frames.
